newsitem.title: USA: IMF defends debt initiative, sees more in pipeline.
newsitem.headline: IMF defends debt initiative, sees more in pipeline.

text.p: The IMF, facing charges a debt write-off plan for poor nations is going too slowly, said on Sunday another five or six countries will be lined up to benefit from the initiative in the next few months.

International Monetary Fund official Jack Boorman said that besides debt relief promised to Uganda, decisions were due on Bolivia, Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast shortly, and two or three nations more would be considered in coming months.
He cited Guyana and Mozambique as likely "to be on the agenda reasonably quickly".
He also said that the initiative, which in Africa has been overshadowed by civil war in Zaire, was only a small part of attempts to help the world's poorest nations.
"They are faced with numerous problems and debt is one of them and this initiative is aimed at that particular problem. It is a piece of a very large pie," said Boorman.
He said the IMF would look closely at defense expenditures in countries likely to benefit to make sure money from debt relief was not diverted to arms.

Concern about an increase in military spending by Uganda, alleged to be helping rebels fighting to oust President Mobutu Sese Seko in Zaire, had been a sticking point in talks on giving it debt relief, officials have said.

World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Friday Uganda had been warned about such outlays and said he had received assurances debt relief funds, meant to go to schools, hospitals and other social purposes, would not be diverted.

The IMF and World Bank approved the debt relief for Uganda last week, making it the first to benefit from the initiative, which is being carried out jointly with the Paris Club of creditor nations and other multilateral lenders.
Around 15 to 20 countries, mostly in Africa, are expected to benefit, at a total cost to their creditors estimated at between $5.5 billion and $8.4 billion.

The initiative, however, has been criticized by aid agencies who say the procedures for approving and providing debt relief are too slow. Uganda will not get its relief of around $340 million until next April.
Development watchdog group Eurodad said discussions on the first countries fuelled fears that most nations in need of debt relief would only receive it beyond the year 2000.
"The amount of money at stake for creditors does not justify the continued existence of millions of people in abject poverty," Eurodad added in a statement.

The Group of 24 developing nations, meeting on the fringes of the IMF/World Bank spring gathering, on Sunday said that while it appreciated the HIPC effort, more funds and more flexible terms were needed.

In a communique issued after their meeting, the G24 warned that "prolongued delays in dealing with the debt overhang (of the poorest nations) will undermine the effectiveness of the initiative ... and erode domestic political support".
But Boorman said the procedures were needed for a fair assessment of a country's right to qualify for debt relief.
He noted the IMF and World Bank had agreed to broaden criteria for qualifying for the debt relief to allow countries with open economies and strong exports to benefit.
These would have been excluded by a requirement that debt service charges be 200 to 250 percent of export revenues.
Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said on Saturday these broader guidelines should allow Ivory Coast, Guyana, Yemen, Congo and Mauritania to benefit.
